rationale: Within-site AUROC means only within-cohort ranking counts, but the pooled model is fit on four cohorts, so large between-site shifts in protein levels (pre-analytics, instrument runs) can pull its coefficients toward site directions. This change centres each protein per site, using medians from the training fold (an additive shift per site), so the regularized logistic regression learns diagnosis contrasts inside each cohort rather than between cohorts.

CSF proteomics studies of AD (Bader 2020, Higginbotham/Johnson modules) repeatedly find the same markers: tau-correlated glycolytic enzymes and 14-3-3 proteins (SMOC1, YWHAG, PKM, ALDOA, GAPDH, ENO, MDH1), neuronal injury and synaptic proteins (NEFL, NRGN, NPTX2, VGF), and glial/inflammatory proteins (CHI3L1, SPP1, GFAP, TREM2, complement, APOE/CLU). After standardization I multiply these prior-biology features by 2, which cuts their L2 penalty by 4x. With only ~110 training samples, the ridge-logistic model should then use well-validated biology before noise proteins, while still being able to use every protein.

Several key AD CSF markers (NEFL, SMOC1, NPTX2, CHIT1, TREM2, GFAP, NRGN) are low in abundance, so DIA often fails to quantify them. The 70% completeness filter therefore probably drops some of them before the prior can help. This change keeps prior-biology proteins that are quantified in at least 30% of training samples. Their missing values get half-minimum imputation, which treats "not detected" as "low abundance" (the data are missing not at random), so the downweighted-penalty model can use these markers.

I'm adding three explicit module scores built from groups of markers that move in the same direction in AD CSF: the tau-correlated glycolysis/14-3-3/SMOC1 module (up), the glial-activation module (CHI3L1/CHIT1/SPP1/GFAP/TREM2, up) and the neuronal secretory/synaptic module (NPTX2/NPTXR/VGF/SCG2/CHGA, down). Each score is the mean of its proteins' standardized values, so measurement noise should average out and the logistic regression gets a low-variance summary of each module, with the same weak penalty as the prior markers.

I'm adding a second group of tau-correlated glycolytic and metabolic proteins to the low-penalty biology prior. These come from Bader 2020 and the Higginbotham/Johnson "sugar metabolism" CSF module: GOT1, LDHA, PGAM1, PPIA, PARK7, FABP3, TMSB10, TMSB4X, GDA and CD44. Adding the three module scores in round 4 didn't help, but weighting single known markers more strongly did (round 2). So giving more of these co-regulated, well-replicated proteins the 4x weaker penalty should give the model more independent noisy readouts of the same tau/neurodegeneration signal.

Per-sample median centring currently takes the median over whichever proteins were quantified in each sample. DIA missingness depends on abundance, so samples with fewer detected low-abundance proteins get an artificially higher median, and normalization then shifts every protein in those samples. Taking the median only over the core of proteins quantified in at least 95% of samples gives each sample its normalization factor from the same set of proteins. That should give a cleaner correction for CSF dilution and loading. The core set is chosen without labels.

CSF samples carry varying amounts of blood contamination. Many of the prior proteins are also highly abundant in red blood cells (GAPDH, ENO1, PKM, ALDOA, LDHA, PGK1, TPI1, PPIA, PARK7, SOD1, PEBP1, the 14-3-3 proteins), so contamination adds per-sample noise to exactly the features the model relies on. This change builds a label-free hemoglobin/carbonic-anhydrase contamination score and removes its linear effect from every protein before modelling, to recover the brain-derived signal.

Round 1's per-site centring probably failed because it used plain per-site medians. AD prevalence differs by cohort, so subtracting a site's median also removed part of the disease signal. This version subtracts a class-balanced site centre instead: the midpoint of that site's AD and non-AD mean, taken from training-fold labels only and then applied to test samples from the same site. That removes cohort-level pre-analytic shifts but keeps the within-site AD contrast, which is exactly what the within-site AUROC rewards.

Removing the erythrocyte-contamination axis helped in round 7. Platelets are the other main contamination source in CSF taps (Geyer 2019 quality-marker panels), and they are rich in thymosins, glycolytic enzymes and 14-3-3 proteins, several of which are in the low-penalty prior. So this change builds a second label-free score from platelet-specific proteins (PF4, PPBP, ITGA2B, GP1BA and others) and regresses it out of every protein after the blood axis. The aim is to reduce per-sample noise in the prior features.

The 4x weaker penalty on the biology prior gave the largest gain so far (round 2), but the prior strength (2x feature scale) and C were fixed by hand. This change picks PRIOR_SCALE ∈ {1.5, 2, 3} and C ∈ {0.03, 0.05, 0.1} on each training fold. It scores them with grouped inner CV (`groups_train`), using within-site AUROC to match the metric, so the balance between known AD CSF markers and all other proteins is set by the data and not by guesswork.

This change adds the rest of the CSF neurosecretory/synaptic peptide module to the low-penalty prior: CHGB, SCG3, SCG5, PCSK1N, PCSK1, PENK, PDYN, SST, NRN1, CBLN4, NPTX1, CRH and CARTPT. Johnson/Higginbotham CSF proteomics and older SST studies report these consistently lower in AD, and they track cognitive decline more closely than tau does. Round 5 showed that extending the prior with co-regulated, well-replicated markers helps, so this should add more independent, reliable readouts of synaptic loss. The inner-CV tuning of prior strength and C stays the same.

Inner CV picks one (prior-scale, C) pair from 9 using within-site AUROC on about 110 samples split over 4 cohorts, so the pick is noisy. This change averages the predicted probabilities of the 3 best inner-CV configurations instead of using only the single best. That should keep the data-driven prior strength while lowering the variance of a single noisy selection under small n.

Cohorts differ in AD prevalence, and the pooled logistic regression is fit across all four, so protein shifts between sites become correlated with the label. The model can then spend coefficients on those cohort directions, which cannot help a within-site AUROC. Rounds 1 and 8 tried to fix this by centring each site, which removed real signal. This change leaves the features alone and instead weights training samples so that AD and non-AD carry equal total weight inside each site, which breaks the site–label correlation. The weights use training-fold labels only and are applied in both the inner CV and the final fit.

With only about 110 training samples, a few extreme protein values can dominate the L2-logistic coefficients and the test-set rankings. These come from failed quantifications, residual contamination, or the half-minimum imputed floor for sparsely detected prior markers. This change winsorizes every standardized feature to ±3 SD using training-fold statistics, so single samples have bounded influence and the model has to rely on consistent shifts across samples.

Inner-CV selection of (prior scale, C) currently uses one GroupKFold partition of about 110 samples across 4 cohorts, so which configuration wins depends heavily on how subjects fall into folds. This change repeats the grouped inner CV over 3 seeded random group-to-fold assignments and picks the configuration with the best mean within-site AUROC, which should give a lower-variance choice of the biology-prior strength under small n.

With about 110 training samples and over 1,000 correlated proteins, the L2-logistic model sits close to a max-margin fit and its coefficients have high variance. This change blends it with a diagonal LDA score, a much lower-variance estimator: the sum over proteins of the standardized AD vs non-AD mean difference times the z-scored value, with the same biology-prior boost. Both scores are z-scored using training-fold statistics before blending, and the blend weight (0 / 0.25 / 0.5) is picked by the existing grouped inner CV with within-site AUROC, so it can fall back to pure logistic. I haven't run this candidate, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

The diagonal-LDA part of the blend currently sums standardized mean differences over about 1,000 proteins, and most of them are pure noise (sampling SE of d ≈ 0.2 at n≈110), which adds variance to the score. This change turns it into a nearest-shrunken-centroid (PAM, Tibshirani 2002) score: each protein's effect is soft-thresholded by δ·SE, with δ ∈ {0, 1, 2} chosen together with the blend weight by the existing grouped inner CV on within-site AUROC. Noise proteins drop out and consistent markers remain. δ=0 reproduces the current model.

The diagonal-LDA part of the blend currently estimates each protein's effect from pooled AD vs non-AD means. AD prevalence differs between cohorts, so site-level shifts leak into those means, and the score is only judged on rankings within each site. This change estimates the effect from within-site contrasts instead: a Mantel-Haenszel-style weighted average of per-site mean differences, divided by the within-site/within-class pooled SD. Only training-fold labels are used, the features are left untouched (unlike rounds 1 and 8), and the existing inner CV can still set the blend weight to 0.

Clipping standardized features at ±3 SD helped (round 14). That suggests that, even after log2, protein distributions are skewed and heavy-tailed, and the imputed half-minimum floor adds big tied blocks of values. This change goes one step further and replaces z-scoring with a rank-based inverse-normal transform fitted on the training fold. Test samples are mapped by interpolating the training-set empirical CDF. The result is re-standardized and then clipped as before. Each protein then contributes only its order, Spearman-style, so no tail value or imputation floor can dominate the L2-logistic or diagonal-LDA scores, while "not detected = lowest" is kept.

The round-19 rank-inverse-normal transform turns the half-minimum imputed floor into one bounded, tied lowest-rank block, so sparsely quantified proteins can no longer produce extreme values. Many brain-derived CSF proteins are low-abundance and missing not at random, so I'm relaxing the generic completeness filter from 70% to 50% to let them in, with "not detected = lowest rank". I haven't run this change, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.
